subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Second Wave: Starbucks Era
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Second Wave: Starbucks Era.

hook.text: In 1971, three friends opened a small coffee shop in Seattle's Pike Place Market. They named it Starbucks.

buildup.text: Howard Schultz visited Italian espresso bars in 1983 and saw something Starbucks wasn't doing: selling drinks.

discovery.text: Schultz bought the company and turned it into an espresso bar chain. The latte went mainstream.

twist.text: Starbucks didn't just sell coffee—it sold a 'third place' between home and work. The café experience mattered.

climax.text: By 2000, Starbucks had 3,500 stores. Today it has over 35,000 worldwide.

punchline.text: An Italian idea, scaled in Seattle, served worldwide.

quiz.question: What inspired Howard Schultz to transform Starbucks?

details.summary: The second wave, launched by Peet's Coffee and perfected by Starbucks, introduced Americans to espresso drinks, origin awareness, and coffee as a lifestyle. Starbucks grew from one Seattle store in 1971 to a global empire. It created the concept of the cafe as a third place between home and work.
details.whyItMatters: The second wave elevated coffee from anonymous commodity to branded experience. It educated millions of consumers and created the foundation for specialty coffee.
takeaways: The second wave began with Peet's Coffee in 1966
Starbucks popularized espresso drinks and cafe culture
It created the third place concept for coffee shops

faq.question: What did Starbucks change about coffee culture?
faq.answer: Starbucks taught Americans to order espresso drinks by name, pay premium prices for coffee, and spend time in cafes. It introduced customization, seasonal offerings, and coffee as a lifestyle brand. The company's store design, music, and atmosphere made the experience as important as the drink.

faq.question: How did the second wave lead to the third wave?
faq.answer: By educating consumers about espresso, origin, and willingness to pay more, Starbucks created a market for even higher quality. Third-wave roasters differentiated by offering what Starbucks could not: single-origin transparency, lighter roasts, and artisanal preparation.
